passage: The lemon-and-spoon race at the Bhatpara fair was over in a minute. Sharmila's lemon rolled into the dust just before the line, and three girls ran past her. She stood still, then burst into loud, angry tears. Her aunt Minakshi pushed through the crowd and knelt beside her. She didn't say "don't cry." She held Sharmila's dusty hands and said, "You were so fast. That's why it hurts so much." Sharmila cried into her aunt's shoulder until her breathing slowed. They shared a paper cone of roasted chana. When the teacher called for the second heat, Sharmila looked up. "Can I go again?" Minakshi wiped her face with the end of her dupatta. "Hold the spoon a little lower this time." Sharmila ran. She finished fourth, grinning.

qa.q: What happened to Sharmila's lemon in the first race?
qa.a: It rolled into the dust just before the line, and three girls ran past her.

qa.q: Why do you think Sharmila felt ready to ask "Can I go again?"
qa.a: Her aunt had stayed close, let her cry and told her the hurt made sense, so the loss no longer felt too big. Feeling safe gave her the courage to try.

qa.q: Minakshi could have told Sharmila to stop crying. What did she choose instead, and why did it help?
qa.a: She knelt, held her hands and said the hurt made sense because Sharmila had been so fast. Being understood calmed Sharmila faster than being told to stop.

qa.q: How might Minakshi have felt when Sharmila finished fourth, grinning?
qa.a: She was probably proud and relieved, because the girl who had been crying in the dust was now happy to have tried again. 😊

grounding: A girl who loses a race cries, is comforted by her aunt, and then runs the second heat with a grin.

passage: In their flat in Valencia, Tomas lost at chess to his big brother Mateo for the sixth time that week. His king was trapped in the corner. Tomas swept the pieces off the board and ran to the balcony, crying hard. Mateo followed. He didn't laugh. He sat on the cold tiles next to his brother and waited. After a while he said, "When I was nine, I threw the whole board at Papá." Tomas sniffed. "Really?" "Really. Losing feels awful. You're allowed to be mad." They watched the scooters below for a bit. Then Mateo said, "Want me to show you how I trapped your king?" Tomas nodded. They picked up the pieces together. The next game lasted twice as long, and Tomas took Mateo's queen.

qa.q: Where did Tomas run after sweeping the pieces off the board?
qa.a: He ran to the balcony, crying hard.

qa.q: What did Tomas probably feel when Mateo said he once threw the whole board at Papá?
qa.a: He likely felt less ashamed and less alone, because even his big brother had felt that angry. His "Really?" shows he was surprised and starting to calm.

qa.q: What was the turning point that got Tomas back to the board?
qa.a: Mateo sat with him without laughing and said losing feels awful, then offered to show him the trap. Being accepted first made him willing to learn.

qa.q: What is it like for Mateo to keep beating his younger brother?
qa.a: He may feel a little guilty or unsure how to help. Sitting on the balcony and sharing his own story lets him be a brother instead of just the winner.

grounding: A boy who loses at chess cries on the balcony, his older brother comforts him, and he plays again.

passage: At the Saturday badminton club in the community centre, Santosh, ten, lost his first match 21–6. He walked off the court, sat against the wall and pulled his cap down, shoulders shaking. Coach Hansa finished calling scores, then sat on the floor next to him in silence. "That was a tough one," she said quietly. Santosh wiped his nose on his wrist. "I'm the worst." "You're upset. Of course you are. You wanted it." She gave him her water bottle. "I lost a lot at your age. I cried in the changing room every week." He peeked from under the cap. "Every week?" "Nearly." Then she said, "Court three's free. Want to hit some drops with me?" He stood up. They rallied until the lights clicked off.

qa.q: What was the score of Santosh's first match?
qa.a: He lost his first match 21–6.

qa.q: What does Santosh's cap pulled down suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: He was ashamed and did not want others to see him crying. He felt like "the worst" after the loss.

qa.q: Coach Hansa sat with Santosh before suggesting more play. Why was that timing a good choice?
qa.a: If she had pushed him back on court at once, he might have felt his tears did not matter. Waiting and naming his feelings first made trying again feel safe.

qa.q: How might the other children at the club see Coach Hansa after this?
qa.a: They may see her as someone who stays with you when you lose, not only when you win. That can make them less afraid of losing in front of her.

grounding: A boy who loses a badminton match cries, is comforted by his coach, and goes back to practise with her.

passage: I'm Seema, Jomon's big sister. On Sunday the colony boys played football, and Jomon's team lost because his penalty hit the post. He stood there, then burst into tears and ran to Appachan on the bench. I thought Appachan would say, "Don't cry, be a man." He didn't. He put his arm round Jomon and said, "That hurt, didn't it? I'm right here." Jomon cried into his shirt for a long time. Appachan just waited. Then Jomon wiped his face and asked, "Can I take one more kick, just practice?" Appachan went in goal. Jomon scored. I think the hug came first, and the kick came after.

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling when he ran to Appachan?
qa.a: He felt hurt and upset, maybe ashamed that his miss cost the game, and he wanted comfort from someone safe.

qa.a: He named the hurt and stayed close instead of telling Jomon not to cry, so Jomon felt safe enough to ask for one more kick.

qa.q: How did watching this change what Seema expected from Appachan?
qa.a: Seema expected a "be a man" remark, so seeing a hug and patience showed her that comfort, not scolding, helped her brother try again.

passage: Baljeet, you cried when you lost the cricket match today? Come, sit. Let me tell you about the kho-kho final when I was a girl of nine, in our school in Amritsar. We lost by one point, and it was my fault. I was caught at the last second. I ran behind the school wall and cried so hard I couldn't breathe. My father found me. He didn't say, "Stop crying." He sat on the ground in his good trousers and held me. "You're sad. That's okay. I'm here." I cried until it was finished. Then he wiped my face and said, "Shall we practise that dodge tomorrow?" I nodded. The next morning we practised in the courtyard. The next year, we won. Shalini's secret, beta: it's easier to try again when someone holds you first.

qa.q: Where did young Shalini run to cry?
qa.a: Behind the school wall.

qa.q: How did young Shalini feel after her father held her?
qa.a: Shalini felt safe enough to cry until the sadness finished, then calm and willing to try again.

qa.q: What choice in the story helped Shalini bounce back?
qa.a: Her father chose to hold her and name her sadness instead of telling her to stop crying, then offered practice together the next day.

qa.q: How might Shalini's father have felt sitting on the ground in his good trousers?
qa.a: He probably felt tender and sad for her, caring more about comforting her than about his clothes.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how, as a child, being comforted after losing a game made it safe to feel sad and then try again.

passage: The inter-school chess tournament in Chennai was held in a crowded hall with fans that barely worked. Karthik, eight, lost his second game in twelve moves. He walked out to the corridor, face hot, and started crying behind a pillar. His mother Disha was supposed to be there, but she was stuck in traffic. A volunteer sat near him. Twenty minutes later Disha rushed in, breathless, and found him. She knelt and hugged him. "You lost. That hurts." Karthik sobbed into her shoulder. She waited, rubbing his back. When he was calm, she gave him a banana and said, "Round three starts in ten minutes. Do you want to play?" He sniffed. "What if I lose again?" "Then I'll hug you again." Karthik laughed a little, wiped his nose, and walked back to the board.

qa.q: How many moves did Karthik's second game last?
qa.a: Twelve moves.

qa.q: How did Karthik feel after his mother's hug?
qa.a: Karthik felt comforted and calm enough to laugh a little, safe to try again because his mother would be there either way.

qa.q: What did Disha's response get right?
qa.a: She named his hurt, let him cry without rushing, and then offered the next round with the promise of support, not pressure.

qa.q: How might the volunteer have felt waiting near Karthik?
qa.a: The volunteer may have felt concerned and relieved when his mother finally arrived.

grounding: It shows a child who cries after losing a game, is comforted by his mother, and then tries again, with warmth making hard feelings safe.

passage: On the Sunday after Diwali, Chetan, ten, played carrom with the older boys in the building in Pune. He lost every game. After the last one, he threw the striker and ran upstairs. Rehana aunty from next door, who had watched, followed him. She found him on the stairs, crying into his knees. She sat beside him. "Losing three times in a row. That's hard." He nodded without looking up. She didn't tell him to stop. She just stayed. After a while he said, "They're all better than me." "They're older. They've played longer. You got two coins on the first shot, I saw." He looked up. "You saw that?" "I did. Want to practise that shot with me tomorrow?" Chetan wiped his face. The next evening he was back at the board, lips pressed together, aiming carefully.

qa.q: How many games did Chetan lose?
qa.a: He lost every game, three in a row.

qa.q: How did Chetan feel when Rehana aunty mentioned the two coins?
qa.a: He felt surprised and a bit comforted that she had noticed something he did well, which made trying again feel possible.

qa.q: How did Rehana aunty help Chetan bounce back?
qa.a: She sat with him, named his hurt, stayed quietly, pointed out a real strength, and offered to practise together.

qa.q: How might the older boys see Chetan coming back the next evening?
qa.a: They might be surprised and impressed that he returned after losing every game.

grounding: It shows a child who cries after losing a game, is comforted by a warm neighbour, and then tries again.

"Hey, hey," Chetan bhaiya said, coming round to his side. "Come here."

Madhav sniffed. "It was lucky."

"Play again? I'll show you how I aim."

I'm Zeenat. Last Saturday I lost in the second round of the school chess tournament.

I moved my knight without looking and Amandeep took my queen. When we shook hands my eyes went blurry and I ran to the corridor.

Ms Pereira came out. She didn't say "don't cry". She sat on the bench next to me and said, "That hurts, doesn't it?" I nodded and cried properly. She just waited.

Then she asked, "Want to see what happened?" We set up the board and she showed me the knight move. "You'll never do that one again," she said.

After lunch there was a friendly game for everyone who was out. I almost didn't go, but I did. I lost that one too, but not because of my knight.

qa.q: Who took Zeenat's queen?
qa.a: Amandeep took Zeenat's queen.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling after shaking hands with Amandeep?
qa.a: Zeenat felt upset and disappointed, with eyes going blurry, and ran to the corridor to cry.

qa.q: What did Ms Pereira do that another adult could copy?
qa.a: Ms Pereira named the hurt, waited while Zeenat cried, then looked at the mistake calmly, which made trying again feel safe.

qa.q: How might Amandeep have felt when Zeenat ran to the corridor?

passage:
Coach's note, junior athletics, Friday

Chetan came fifth in the 400 metres today. He had been sure of a medal. At the finish he walked straight to the fence, pulled his cap down and cried hard.

I stood next to Chetan and didn't talk at first. When he looked up I said, "You really wanted this one." He said, "I'm the worst." I told him I'd seen him run his best time at the second bend, and that fifth out of twelve was a real race.

Then I asked: relay leg later, or sit out? He thought about it and said, "Run."

He ran it well and came back grinning. I've told his parents about both races, the tears and the relay.

Sachin

qa.q: What position did Chetan come in the 400 metres?
qa.a: Chetan came fifth in the 400 metres.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling when he said "I'm the worst"?
qa.a: Chetan felt crushed and ashamed after missing the medal he was sure of, so he saw himself as the worst.

qa.q: How did Sachin handle the moment well?
qa.a: Sachin stayed close without lecturing, named the wish, gave honest encouragement and let Chetan choose the relay.

qa.q: How might Chetan's parents feel reading about both races?
qa.a: Chetan's parents might feel touched by the tears and proud that he chose to run again.

grounding: A coach notes a child who cries after losing a race, is comforted and then chooses to run again.

Today I, Chaitanya, lost the carrom final to my cousin Jatin. I was one coin away. Then I missed the queen and he pocketed everything.
I threw the striker and ran to my room and cried into my pillow. I felt so stupid.
Amma came in. She didn't say "it's just a game." She sat on my bed and rubbed my back and said, "You wanted it so much. That's why it hurts." I cried more, but it was a better kind of crying.
After a while she brought me a glass of water. Then she said, "Shall we practise the queen shot together?"
We played for half an hour. I got the queen three times.
In the evening I asked Jatin for a rematch. I lost again. But only by two coins. Tomorrow I'm winning.

On Sankranti, the sky over the village was full of kites. Shankar, eight, had flown his green kite since morning, until an older boy's string cut it loose. He watched it drift over the sugarcane fields. Then he sat down on the roof and howled.
His uncle Divyansh didn't tell him to stop. He sat down next to him on the warm tiles and put an arm around him. "That was your best kite. Of course you're sad."
Shankar cried into his shirt until the crying slowed.
Divyansh-chacha unwrapped a new kite, a yellow one he had been saving. "Shall we try? I'll hold the reel. You fly."
Shankar sniffed, wiped his nose, and nodded.
By evening, the yellow kite was high, and Shankar was shouting at the boy next door, "Come and try to cut this one!"

qa.q: What colour was the kite that got cut?
qa.a: It was green.

qa.q: How did Shankar feel when his uncle said "Of course you're sad"?
qa.a: He felt comforted and safe to keep crying, which helped the crying slow down.

qa.q: What did Divyansh-chacha do well to help Shankar try again?
qa.a: He comforted Shankar first, then offered a new kite and to hold the reel, so trying again felt shared and safe.

qa.q: How might the older boy next door feel when Shankar challenges him?
qa.a: He might be surprised and amused that Shankar is back, bold and ready to play.

grounding: It shows a child who lost a kite fight crying, being comforted warmly and then trying again, as resilience starts with a safe relationship.

It was Tết in Hanoi, and the community centre held a children's chess tournament. Tuan, nine, lost his third game in eleven moves. He knocked over his king, pushed back his chair and ran to the corridor, crying.
Fatima, the volunteer coach, found him by the window. She knelt down. "Losing hurts. Especially when you tried hard."
"I'm bad at chess," he sobbed.
"You're sad right now. That's okay. Sit with me a minute."
She didn't hurry him. She held out a tissue and waited while the crying slowed.
Then she said, "There's one more round. Do you want to play, or watch with me?"
Tuan thought. "Play," he whispered.
He lost that one too, but in thirty moves. When he came out, he ran to Fatima. "I lasted so long!"

qa.q: How many moves did Tuan's third game last?
qa.a: It lasted eleven moves.

qa.q: How did Tuan feel after Fatima sat with him?
qa.a: He felt calmer and safe enough to try again, after first feeling sad and sure he was bad at chess.

qa.q: Why did Fatima's approach help Tuan bounce back?
qa.a: She named his sadness as okay and waited without rushing, then gave him a choice, which let him return to play on his own terms.

qa.q: How might Fatima feel when Tuan runs to her after the last game?
qa.a: Fatima would probably feel happy and proud, seeing him excited about lasting thirty moves.

grounding: It shows a child who lost a game crying, being comforted by a warm adult and then choosing to play again, as resilience begins with a safe relationship.

The sports club hall was cold that January morning, and everyone kept their sweaters on for the table-tennis ladder. Damini lost her match to a younger boy, 11–4. She put the bat down and her face crumpled. Big tears came.
Coach Amandeep didn't tell her to stop crying. He knelt beside the bench. "Losing hurts, na? You really wanted that one."
Damini nodded, wiping her nose on her sleeve. He sat with her, not talking, while the next match started. After a while he said, "Your backhand was good today. Want to try one more game with me before lunch?"
She sniffed. Then she picked the bat up. The first ball went into the net. The second one went over, and she almost smiled.
